how: A request for a sprite and a concrete shark proposal give contributors something to build.
Participants propose a timed build and later recruit defenders.
Recruitment concerns active contributors rather than nominal subscribers, since even half a percent running the script is presented as sufficient.
Proposed sprite size is constrained by the space contributors believe they can find and maintain.
One contributor temporarily stopping from exhaustion must be distinguished from a collective decision to abandon the work.
Contributors debate how bow, blush, lipstick and eye details make a workable shark recognisably theirs.
Builders report a started nose and outline work while checking and correcting the blue.
A template provides a concrete target that can be trimmed to spare a neighbour.
Contributors share and run a defence script and propose throwaway accounts to bypass the placement wait.
A common target updates every script runner automatically, giving contributors a technical means of coordinating placement changes.
A script recipient reports an instance running in one line without asking anything back.
An explicit leader disclaimer can coexist with coordinated placement through an automatically updated target, so lack of appointed command does not imply wholly dispersed practical control.
A visibility thread is redirected toward defending the existing masterpiece rather than adding more.
Participants identify intended bow pixels being fixed and distinguish that problem from random vandalism.
Contributors accommodate overlap and trim their template to avoid conflict with neighbouring art.
Participants offer reciprocal limits on rays, background and border pixels, then report an agreement failing.
A neighbour offers five accounts for a chosen repair template, establishing offered help but not its delivery.
A self-described active member answers an external negotiating approach with a concession despite denying leadership.
The leader request and disclaimer instantiate the element's narrow request range without demonstrating disagreement over whether an agreement binds members.
